title: What happens during a lumbar puncture?
intro: A lumbar puncture, or spinal tap, is a procedure in which a thin needle is inserted into the lower back to collect cerebrospinal fluid, the liquid around the brain and spinal cord. It helps diagnose infections, bleeding, inflammation and some neurological diseases.

sections.heading: Why it is done
paragraphs: The fluid can show meningitis, bleeding around the brain, multiple sclerosis, nerve inflammation and some cancers. It is sometimes used to measure pressure or to give medicines, for instance in some cancer treatments or for anaesthesia. A scan may be done first to be sure the procedure is safe.

sections.heading: Before the procedure
paragraphs: You will be asked about blood-thinning medicines, which may need to be paused, and allergies. The procedure is explained and you give consent. Tests may check blood clotting. You can usually eat and drink beforehand, and you can empty your bladder.

sections.heading: During the procedure
paragraphs: You lie on your side curled up, or sit leaning forward, to open the spaces between the bones of the spine. The back is cleaned and numbed with local anaesthetic. A needle is inserted below the end of the spinal cord, so it does not damage it. A few millilitres of fluid are collected. It usually takes fifteen to thirty minutes.

sections.heading: Afterwards and risks
paragraphs: You are asked to lie flat for a short time and drink fluids. A headache, which is worse when upright and better lying down, affects some people for a few days. Back pain or tenderness may occur. Rare risks include infection, bleeding, nerve irritation and brain herniation if pressure is high. Seek help for severe headache, fever, numbness or weakness in the legs.

sections.heading: Results
paragraphs: Some results, such as cell counts, are available within hours, while others take days. The doctor will explain what the findings mean for diagnosis and treatment. Ask about follow-up and any restrictions on activity.

examples.title: Staying comfortable
examples.text: Imagine you are lying on your side for the procedure. You could breathe slowly, tell the doctor if you feel pain and try to stay still.

examples.title: Recovering at home
examples.text: Suppose you develop a headache the next day. You might rest lying down, drink fluids and call if it is severe or does not improve.
